stories.title: Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller
stories.summary: Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise , offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative. It’s essentially a portmanteau biopic: its hero is Cui Xun, a fictional stand-in for the venerable Cui Daozhi , a still-extant real-life figure who so revolutionised forensic science he became known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. Ripping three-and-a-bit tales from the casebook – involving a 1970s child killer, a grisly 1980s multiple murder and a 1990s bus bombing (plus one lingering loose end), Chen constructs a history of forensic investigation that is also, in variably oblique ways, a history of Chinese law enforcement, which is shown evolving from boozy, gloveless crime-scene trampling to something far more streamlined and professional. Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases

T he latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise , offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative. It’s essentially a portmanteau biopic: its hero is Cui Xun, a fictional stand-in for the venerable Cui Daozhi , a still-extant real-life figure who so revolutionised forensic science he became known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. Ripping three-and-a-bit tales from the casebook – involving a 1970s child killer, a grisly 1980s multiple murder and a 1990s bus bombing (plus one lingering loose end), Chen constructs a history of forensic investigation that is also, in variably oblique ways, a history of Chinese law enforcement, which is shown evolving from boozy, gloveless crime-scene trampling to something far more streamlined and professional.

Within the handsome period framework, Chen follows the science: one era’s crazy innovation becomes commonplace in the next. A rookie Cui (played here by Zhang Yi, ageing up subtly) uses boiled potatoes to take dental imprints; when these run out, he and his colleagues start biting one another’s cheeks to make their points. (Their scars are a terrific visual gag: scientists literally showing their working.) By the 90s, when Cui is heading a team working out of a vast, well-staffed warehouse, we seem mere moments away from David Caruso’s sunglasses and memorable Who guitar riffs. The forbidding subtext is presumably that, after 50 years of such breakthroughs, there’s no more getting away with it; as one suspect insists: “everyone pays for what they’ve done.”

Yet Chen’s impressively limber storytelling also accommodates thumping set pieces and knotty forensic puzzle-solving. Remaining necessarily alert to key details, Zhang, in a likable unshowy turn, really does look like someone who’s spent long afternoons studying fingernail structure. The character’s personal life soon drifts out of focus, but the wider picture compels: a culture both becoming more baroque in its sociopathy – the bus bombers are an Asian equivalent to Leopold and Loeb – and sharpening its eye. (End titles also cite the centrality of Cui’s work to China’s current surveillance schemes.) Chen is pursuing reassuring closure and creates an arresting, effective feature besides.

stories.title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
stories.summary: Ukraine competes with Russia and data centers for China’s optical fiber supply.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ukraine competes with Russia and data centers for China’s optical fiber supply.

Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones.

Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider .

Ukraine and Russia have been producing an estimated 50,000 fiber-optic drones per month in recent years. That’s a lot of optical fiber that has effectively become a one-time battlefield consumable.

But China’s economic and security ties with Russia have enabled Russia to import significantly larger amounts of fiber-optic cable than Ukraine—at least according to China’s official customs data. For example, Russia imported 328,000 miles of fiber-optic cable from China in August 2025 alone, compared to Ukraine getting just 72 miles of cable from Chinese companies, according to The Washington Post .

To get a better sense of how drone warfare has increased demand for optical fiber technology, Russia alone bought more than 37 million miles (60 million kilometers) of fiber-optic cable in 2025, according to The Insider and Russian business publication Vedomosti . That means Russia’s purchases amounted to more than 10 percent of all fiber produced worldwide last year, when it had previously never accounted for more than 1 percent of global demand.

The global AI boom and ongoing data center buildout have also strained optical fiber supply, with an expected worldwide shortfall of 111 million miles (180 million kilometers) in 2026, according to the market research firm TrendForce . That has further increased the cost of optical fiber purchased by Russia and Ukraine, including the bend-insensitive fiber that is especially coveted for fiber-optic drones.

One Ukrainian drone manufacturer navigating these supply-chain challenges is BlueBird Tech, which produces fiber-optic drones along with other military drones, a ground robot, drone detection systems, and electronic warfare systems. Ars reached out to BlueBird Tech to learn more.

The following Q&A represents written responses from Oleksiy, a BlueBird Tech R&D representative, after an initial conversation with Ars. The responses have been lightly edited for clarity. Oleksiy is only being identified by first name for security reasons.

Ars Technica: How has the use of fiber-optic drones by Ukraine and Russia evolved, and where does the technology stand today?

Oleksiy: Fiber-optic drones are a specific type of drone used for particular operations. One of their main characteristics is that they do not produce the same radio-frequency (RF) emissions as conventional RF-controlled FPV drones. That means conventional RF detectors cannot detect them in the same way, and electronic warfare systems cannot disrupt their control link in the same way either.

At the same time, fiber-optic drones have their own operational limitations. A pilot who is experienced with a conventional RF-controlled FPV drone cannot necessarily switch immediately to a fiber-optic drone. It requires specific skills, and fiber-optic drones have different flight characteristics.

So there are significant advantages, particularly when operating in an electronic warfare environment, but there are also limitations in terms of operation, pilot training, and cost.

Because of the high density of electronic intelligence and electronic warfare systems on the battlefield, using conventional radio-controlled FPV drones has become increasingly difficult.

Fiber-optic technology provides a way to operate in these conditions, although it also comes with certain limitations.

So today, both sides are using fiber-optic drones on the battlefield, but radio-controlled drones still make up the larger share overall.

Ars Technica: What are the main disadvantages or limitations of fiber-optic drones?

Oleksiy: One of the biggest limitations today is cost. If we compare fiber-optic prices in 2025 and 2026, we have seen increases of roughly six to 10 times. The most difficult period in terms of prices and shortages was around March. Since then, the situation has stabilized to some extent.

But the underlying issue remains that the material primarily comes from China. That means Ukrainian manufacturers depend on Chinese supply, logistics, availability, and pricing.

There is also broader global demand for fiber-optic material. FPV drones are only one application. Data centers around the world consume large amounts of fiber, and the growth of AI infrastructure is also contributing to demand.

So Ukrainian drone manufacturers are operating within a much larger global market for fiber optic, and that affects both availability and price.

Ars Technica: How are Ukrainian manufacturers adapting to these supply-chain and quality challenges?

Oleksiy: One important change is that many manufacturers are moving the spooling process in-house. Instead of buying a finished fiber-optic spool for an FPV drone, they can buy the fiber in much larger spools and produce the smaller drone spools themselves.

This does not remove the dependence on China for the material itself, but it gives manufacturers more control over the finished product.

Quality is a major reason for doing this. We have seen problems and defects in finished spools supplied from China. By doing the spooling themselves, manufacturers can introduce their own quality-control procedures and achieve a more consistent result.

It can also make the finished spool somewhat cheaper than buying a finished product in China and transporting it to Ukraine.

But quality is the most important factor. If a fiber-optic spool has a defect, you can lose the drone, lose the mission, and lose the target.

Fiber optic is also not the only component in this supply chain. Media converters are another component manufacturers need to source, and China is important for that supply as well.

Ars Technica: So Ukrainian companies are buying large quantities of fiber and producing the FPV spools domestically?

Oleksiy: Yes. A manufacturer can buy a large spool of fiber-optic material and then use that material to produce smaller spools designed for FPV drones.

That also allows the manufacturer to perform its own quality checks during production rather than relying entirely on the quality of a finished imported spool.

Ars Technica: Has this become the standard approach across the Ukrainian industry?

Oleksiy: It depends on the manufacturer and on the size of the company. Larger companies may have the resources to do the spooling themselves. That requires spooling equipment, people who understand the process, testing capabilities, and quality control.

Smaller manufacturers may not have those resources. In those cases, they may buy finished spools from larger Ukrainian manufacturers or from suppliers abroad, including China.

So there is no single model across the industry. It largely depends on the scale and capabilities of each manufacturer.

Ars Technica: Can Ukraine source fiber-optic material from countries other than China?

Oleksiy: You can buy fiber-optic material through suppliers in other countries, but in practice China remains the main source in this market.

There can be intermediaries in other countries, and prices can differ depending on the country and the purchasing route.

But in the end, China remains the main source of the fiber-optic material we are talking about.

Ars Technica: Have Ukrainian companies experienced actual shortages or situations where suppliers were unable or unwilling to fill orders?

Oleksiy: Yes, there have been situations like that. It depends on many factors, including how the material is purchased, which supplier is involved, and the logistics.

There have also been cases where Chinese manufacturers have told Ukrainian buyers that they did not have material available for them because they were from Ukraine.

Russia also has more direct logistics with China, so from a practical supply-chain perspective it has an easier route for sourcing this material.

Ars Technica: Are there other important supply-chain challenges beyond availability and price?

Oleksiy: Yes. Logistics is another important factor. Once the material reaches Ukraine, it still has to pass through customs and then be transported to manufacturers.

Air raid alerts can interrupt this process. Customs operations and other parts of the logistics chain may stop during alerts, which adds time before the material reaches the manufacturer. So companies have to take these delays into account when planning production.

There are also security considerations. I cannot discuss specific cases involving attacks on fiber-optic production because of security restrictions. But manufacturers are potential targets for the enemy, so security measures are extremely important for developers, suppliers, and manufacturers.

Ars Technica: Is the physical transportation route from China to Ukraine also a challenge?

Oleksiy: Yes. The route from China to Ukraine is much longer, and that creates challenges in terms of both time and logistics costs.

So the problem is not only obtaining the material itself. Manufacturers also have to account for the time and expense required to transport it over a long distance.

Ars Technica: How do these price, logistics, and supply-chain challenges affect how a drone manufacturer approaches fiber-optic systems?

Oleksiy: Planning becomes extremely important. You need to plan production and logistics together. If you understand your manufacturing requirements in advance, you can plan your logistics and your next orders accordingly.

Having more of the manufacturing process under your own control is also important.

Quality is another major factor. If the fiber has fewer defects, you can produce more usable FPV spools from one large spool of material. If there are many defects, you ultimately produce fewer usable spools from the same amount of fiber.

So production planning, logistics planning, in-house manufacturing capabilities, material quality, and the skills of the people doing the work are all closely connected.

Ars Technica: Does producing fiber-optic spools require specially trained personnel?

Oleksiy: Yes. We do not have universities that specifically train people to manufacture these FPV fiber-optic spools. So it comes down to training, training, and more training.

When people first learn the process, they naturally make mistakes and create defects. They need practical experience to improve.

Training itself also consumes fiber-optic material because people have to practice the actual manufacturing process.

So developing skilled personnel is another part of scaling production. The goal is to develop the skills required to manufacture consistently high-quality spools with as few defects as possible.

Ars Technica: What makes manufacturing a fiber-optic spool technically difficult?

Oleksiy: You need to understand a lot about the fiber itself, about the spooling process, and about what happens when the fiber unwinds from the spool during operation.

Fiber-optic cable is fragile and can be damaged or broken relatively easily. If something goes wrong during manufacturing or while the fiber is unwinding, you can damage the fiber and lose the connection.

That is why practical experience is so important. You need to practice the manufacturing process, and that can require many kilometers of fiber just for training.

The equipment used for spooling also matters. If you use low-quality equipment or the equipment is not configured properly, you can introduce more defects into the finished spool.

So both the equipment and the people operating it affect the quality of the final product.

Ars Technica: How automated is the spooling process?

Oleksiy: It depends on the type of equipment. Some systems require more manual involvement, while others are more automated.

But even with automated equipment, skilled personnel are still required. Someone has to configure the equipment correctly and understand how the process works. The way the system is set up also affects the quality of the finished product.

So automation does not remove the need for expertise.

Ars Technica: How do manufacturers test the quality of finished fiber-optic spools?

Oleksiy: There are different levels of testing. Every finished spool should be checked to make sure the optical link itself is working properly.

But if you want to ensure consistent production quality, that is not enough. You also need to take a portion of the finished spools from a production batch, install them on actual FPV drones, and fly them under real conditions.

That allows you to test not only the optical connection itself, but also whether the finished spool performs properly during an actual flight.

So every spool should undergo link testing, while some of the finished spools from each production batch should also be tested in real flights. That combination is important if you want to maintain consistent quality in production.

stories.title: Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair
stories.summary: The appointment was made after it emerged Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has become the face of the US AI boom.

Published 10 November 2026, 20:03 GMT

Nvidia has hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate the affair between its chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang, a co-founder of Nvidia who has led it to become one of the most valuable companies in the world, admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman outside of his marriage.

The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing. She was an executive at a Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.

Nvidia said on Tuesday that Wachtell attorney Joon Kim was set to lead "a thorough and independent investigation" into Jensen Huang's affair. The FBI is also conducting its own probe.

Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the US artificial intelligence (AI) boom given it is the sole manufacturer of a crucial computer chip required for successfully operating AI tools.

Shares in the company fell to a near-yearly low on Tuesday, wiping more than $500bn (£375bn) off Nvidia's stock market value since Friday, even as tech stocks have recovered since last week's sell-off.

Jensen Huang's relationship with an executive of an Nvidia customer, who is also believed by the US government to be spying for China, has business and national security implications.

Megaspped had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has maintained was investigated and debunked.

According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring of this year warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Beijing has rejected claims that Jensen Huang has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".

US President Donald Trump said Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang and that the Nvidia boss told him "I had no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed the him.

When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

However, the relationship has drawn political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Jensen Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.

The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC.

Committee chair congressman Brian Mast said he would subpoena Jensen Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before the committee, if necessary.

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 23 hours ago

Joon Kim, who will lead Nvidia's investigation, is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focused on fraud and other criminal acts.

Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.

The investigation is expected to be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the sentiment inside Nvidia. It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang.

Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with Nvidia. He has become a key public figure in the devleopment on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.

A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any additional of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’

Cop31 live – latest updates

China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels , and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.

As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.

In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.

Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.

Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”

For autocratic states without free and fair elections , seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.

“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”

He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”

China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.

Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way : “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”

China as a ‘doer and go-getter’

The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows .

Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.

The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.

after newsletter promotion

“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”

Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed .

Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.

The need for trust

China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.

Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”

If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.

Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.

They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.

For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”

stories.summary: The billionaire tech executive finds himself mired in a personal and national security scandal.

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Published 9 November 2026

One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing , according to a New York Times report.

Jensen Huang admitted , external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the affair.

It said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Jensen Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company.

Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.

Who is Alice Huang and what do we know about the affair?

Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - pictured at an event

US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . Her current whereabouts are unknown.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.

However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.

"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.

China has rejected the spying allegations.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters: "The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China."

The New York Times reported in late October that US President Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf.

Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's [Jensen Huang] an honourable guy."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Jensen Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Jensen Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman.

Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy Published 13 hours ago

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond Published 23 hours ago

Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair Published 43 minutes ago

Why does it matter?

Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers.

Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero.

Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

Sunday's revelations may explain why Jensen Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China .

Who is Jensen Huang?

Huang has soared to international importance with his company

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

Jensen Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff.

He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Jensen Huang.

Trump said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him "'Did you have any idea she was a spy?'"

"He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

What investigations are now under way?

Nvidia has launched an independent investigation into the affair and has hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to carry out the probe.

The investigation will be led by former US Attorney for New York's Southern District, Joon Kim.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI was also investigating the affair . The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC.

Jensen Huang has also been asked to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees on 18 November.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee asked the Nvidia chief executive to appear to explain his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

Jensen Huang has yet to say he will comply, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC.

What is Nvidia and how important is it?

There is no clear successor for Huang at Nvidia

Founded by Jensen Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates .

Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch.

"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them," Witt told the BBC.

Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft, now use Nvidia chips.

Currently worth about $4tn, Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world.

For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Jensen Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".

Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake.

There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy.

His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles.

Who is Jensen Huang's wife?

Lori Huang accompanied her husband at the state dinner held by President Donald Trump for his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in September

Jensen Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners.

They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.

In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.

Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

stories.title: Man who lost $308,000 on sports bets sues Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
stories.summary: Lawsuit demands Kalshi return losses because online betting is illegal in Washington.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lawsuit demands Kalshi return losses because online betting is illegal in Washington.

A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington’s ban on online gambling. He’s trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000.

Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright’s “wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that,” said the gambler’s lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright’s case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits.

“Washington has prohibited Internet gambling since 2006. Washington has also provided, since long before that, a statutory cause of action permitting any person who loses money at illegal gambling to recover it from the proprietor for whose benefit the game was conducted,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

Even if Bright’s lawsuit fails, gamblers who lost on Kalshi could get money back through the lawsuits filed by state governments. For example, Washington’s lawsuit against the company said the attorney general “is entitled to recover all money Washingtonians have lost through Defendant Kalshi’s illegal gambling operation” under the state’s Recovery of Money Lost at Gambling Act. Washington already won a court order restricting the kinds of wagers Kalshi can offer in the state, but it took effect after Bright’s losses.

Kalshi says event contracts aren’t gambling

Kalshi wants Bright’s lawsuit to be moved to US District Court for the Western District of Washington, saying it must be tried in a federal court instead of a state one. In an October 30 motion to dismiss Bright’s case, Kalshi argued that he did not lose any money on “gambling.” Kalshi said he lost money on “event contracts,” which Kalshi says can only be regulated by the federal government.

“The contracts which Plaintiff mischaracterizes as gambling are event contracts offered on the Platform subject to the CEA [Commodity Exchange Act], in conformance with the rules and regulations of the CFTC [Commodity Futures Trading Commission], the federal agency which has statutory authority to oversee the CEA,” Kalshi said.

We contacted Bright’s attorney, Michael Daudt, about Kalshi’s court filings and will update this article if we get a response.

“Plaintiff alleges that his activity on the platform was gambling and that he ‘lost,’” Kalshi wrote. “He does not allege that anyone misled him about how the platform worked, what it charged, or the risk that any position might lose. Yet, he now sues KalshiEX and its parent, Kalshi Inc., to recover nearly double his own alleged net realized loss under Washington’s gambling loss-recovery statute, and a theory of unjust enrichment.”

Between June 17 and August 14, 2026, Bright transferred $315,353.94 to Kalshi in 253 separate debits from his checking account, his lawsuit said. Kalshi allegedly collected $5,589.05 in funding fees on those transfers.

Bright made numerous wagers on sporting events including professional baseball games and tennis matches. He apparently put any winnings into new bets, and alleges that “Kalshi’s platform cycled Plaintiff’s deposits through $14,396,457.30 in transactions and assessed and retained $84,062.71 in trading fees on them, equal to 26.7 percent of everything Plaintiff deposited.”

After all his bets, Bright suffered a net loss of $308,781.62, and his account was left with a balance of $983.27. Kalshi said that Bright’s “alleged losses went to counterparties rather than” to Kalshi itself and that Bright’s “positions were matched with counterparties and resolved according to the outcomes of the underlying events.”

“The Complaint does not allege that KalshiEX or Kalshi Inc. was the counterparty to any of Plaintiff’s positions,” Kalshi said.

Kalshi calls itself “a neutral exchange platform” with no financial stake in the outcome of any event. It makes revenue by collecting fees on transactions. But while Kalshi describes itself as a neutral operator and collector of transaction fees, its business model also includes a trading affiliate that places wagers on the platform.

Kalshi’s trading affiliate

Kalshi’s rulebook says its trading affiliate “participates on the Platform and provides liquidity to the Platform by placing orders on either (or both) sides of a market at competitive price levels.” Kalshi says its affiliate only has access to the same public information that other traders on the platform have.

Bright’s lawsuit alleges that Kalshi’s affiliate “took the opposite side of a substantial portion of Plaintiff’s positions,” meaning that “Kalshi and the enterprise under common ownership with it were not a neutral venue but the dealer or player winning within the meaning of [state law], in addition to being the proprietor for whose benefit the wagering was conducted.”

Bright doesn’t know for sure whether Kalshi’s affiliate was on the other side of any of his bets. “The identity of the participant on the opposite side of each of Plaintiff’s positions, and the profit each such participant realized, is information exclusively within Kalshi’s possession,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in August that Nevada can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws. Although that case involved Nevada, the Ninth Circuit’s jurisdiction includes the state of Washington. Bright’s lawsuit quoted the ruling’s finding that “placing sports bets, even when called by another name, is still gambling.”

Although Bright’s lawsuit said his net loss was $308,781.62, he asked for $580,544.98 based on an “event-by-event” calculation derived from a 1950 ruling issued by the Washington Supreme Court. “Computed on the event-by-event basis required by Heitfeld , under which winnings in separate and distinct events may not be offset against losses, the sums Plaintiff lost total $580,544.98,” the lawsuit said.

Bright’s lawsuit said that if the court declines to order $580,544.98 in restitution, it should instead award “all funds Plaintiff transferred to Kalshi and the $89,651.76 in funding and trading fees Kalshi collected.” That would amount to over $405,000.

Kalshi seeks delay until Supreme Court weighs in

In addition to its motion to dismiss the case, Kalshi filed a motion to stay the proceedings at least until the US Supreme Court decides whether to take up a separate case on whether state gambling laws apply to prediction markets. “The orderly course of justice favors a stay because Supreme Court review will settle or simplify every claim and ensure uniform treatment of like suits,” Kalshi told the US district court.

Kalshi has suffered some notable losses in US appeals courts, which found that states can regulate the platform’s event contracts under gambling laws. But federal courts have not unanimously sided with states, and New Jersey asked the Supreme Court to settle the question of whether states can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws.

Kalshi’s motion for a stay in the Bright case noted that Washington government officials are “pursuing overlapping claims” against Kalshi. “The State of Washington is pursuing the same theory, and seeks the same recovery for Mr. Bright, in a case pending before the Superior Court of Washington for King County,” Kalshi wrote.

Kalshi tried to get the state’s case moved to a federal court, but it was sent back to King County Superior Court in May. Washington won a preliminary injunction against Kalshi in August, when a King County judge ordered Kalshi to implement geofencing and stop allowing many types of wagers in the state.

The county court’s order required Kalshi to stop offering or accepting event contracts “related to sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, or mentions” in the state. The injunction did not affect wagers in the commodities, climate, economics, and finance categories.

Bright transferred his funds to Kalshi before the geofencing order took effect. His lawsuit claims that on September 15, he tried to access the app but received a notice that “using this app in your current location is prohibited.”

This article was updated to correct the date the lawsuit was filed .

stories.body:
Closing summary

Shares of Nvidia tumbled 5% on Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang, was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” Nvidia’s announcement of the investigation on Sunday came after its boss admitted that he had an affair with Alice Huang , an executive at Singapore-based datacenter company Megaspeed, who according to the New York Times , US intelligence determined was gathering information for China. The episode has thrown Jensen Huang’s future at the company – and that of Nvidia itself – up in the air, and raises serious questions about US national security – given Jensen Huang’s close relationship with Donald Trump – and what Alice Huang could have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair.

The New York Times reported in ​October that Trump was briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing, but the US president did not act on it. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I have not ​spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.” Trump later added: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.” He said he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.

The New York Times also reported on Monday that a US commerce department investigation into Megaspeed – the data company led by Alice Huang – was halted after Nvidia’s general counsel intervened. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, reportedly contacted the investigators at commerce department to inform them that their boss, Jeff Kessler – a top official – had given Teter permission to request details about their probe into Megaspeed. The case focused on whether the company was smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China. According to current and former government officials, and others familiar with the incident, that the NYT spoke to, some viewed Kessler’s interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the investigation. The case was eventually transferred to the US justice department late last year, but questions remain about Kessler’s discussions with Nvidia, and what information he subsequently relayed to Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary or the wider Trump administration. According to the Times’ sources, the justice department is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed.

US Republican lawmakers expressed alarm over the episode, asking Jensen Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, currently the House minority leader who is poised to become new Speaker next year, said that he ‌wants restrictions on chips sales to China that in a Senate bill to ‌become law as part of ​an annual defence bill. “Clearly Congress needs more information,” about what ⁠happened at Nvidia, ​Jeffries said, ​adding ​that there are “real ​concerns ‌that ​need ​to be addressed with respect to the Nvidia situation.”

Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls, meanwhile, expressed their support for the embattled Nvidia CEO. Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. Maguire argued the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”. “Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted. “Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post. Bill Ackman , the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair. Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.

There’s a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post, wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives + Co., saying that Huang is “not replaceable.” “On the heels of last week’s Blue Tidal Wave this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China,” Ives wrote.

The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information. “The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”

Briefing.com analyst Patrick O’Hare said that Nvidia was being treated as a one-off story by investors for the moment. “In other words, the stock is being penalised for Jensen Huang’s personal transgression, which has invited a great deal of uncertainty into the mix, but the market isn’t caught up in the notion that this situation is going to have a systemic domino effect,” he said.

The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month. A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.

Over in the US Congress, Hakeem Jeffries , currently the House minority leader who is poised to become its new Speaker next year, has said ⁠that Congress ⁠needs answers after reports emerged ⁠ Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted ⁠by a foreign ​intelligence ‌effort.

Jeffries ‌also said he ‌wants restrictions on chips sales to China that in a Senate bill to ‌become law as part of ​an annual defence bill.

“ Clearly Congress needs more information ,” about what ⁠happened at Nvidia, ​Jeffries said, ​adding ​that there are “real ​concerns ‌that ​need ​to be addressed with respect to the Nvidia situation. ”

The AI poster boy, the ‘Chinese spy’ and Trump: how an affair may have harmed US security

Aisha Down and Dan Milmo

Reports that the boss of a cornerstone company in the global AI boom has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort are a big deal, given Jensen Huang ’s close relationship with the US president.

Aside from Jensen Huang’s dented personal reputation after admitting to having an affair with Alice Huang – an alleged Chinese spy - what is the scale of the damage done to Nvidia and US national security?

The story started to emerge last year when the New York Times and Bloomberg raised questions about a Singapore-based buyer of Nvidia’s powerful chips. There were concerns that Megaspeed was flouting US restrictions on AI chip exports to China by diverting some Nvidia inventory to America’s arch AI rival. Nvidia and Megaspeed denied this.

Then last month came a further startling NYT report that Jensen Huang, a Megaspeed executive, had formed a “close relationship” with Ms Huang and that American officials believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. Donald Trump had been told, but decided not to act on the information. It is now evident that the relationship was more than just close.

At the heart of the question of what China might have achieved through Alice Huang is the extremely close relationship between the CEO of the world’s second-most-valuable company and the president of the United States.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia appeared to have successfully leaned on the US commerce department to halt an investigation into potential chip smuggling on the part of Megaspeed . That pressure came through a Trump appointee, who allowed Nvidia to reach out about the case.

Further, Trump has met frequently – at least seven times – with the head of Nvidia since the start of his second term. Huang has flown on Air Force One and taken calls from the president during public events.

Four of their meetings have touched on one of the most sensitive issues in US-China relationships : the controls that the US has put up around the export of the world’s most advanced AI chips, which are almost entirely sold by Nvidia.

The US president first invited Huang to the White House just six days after he was inaugurated, to discuss AI policy and chip exports . The two then met again in July and August of 2025. This was followed by victories for Huang – Trump allowed Nvidia to export previously banned chips to China. Nvidia agreed, in turn, to give the US government 15% of the sales revenue.

Five months later, the tech boss appeared to win another startling concession, days after another meeting with Trump. The president agreed to allow the tech boss to export H200s – a far more powerful chip – to China, in exchange for 25% of the revenue.

It is not unusual for large technology companies to lobby for their preferred policies in Washington; nor is it unusual for Trump to give access – and favourable deals – to men he likes.

But one more thing is now apparent – during this crucial year for his company, Huang was also intimately involved with a reported Chinese spy. The two were first photographed together in mid-2024. Five months after Trump took office is when the two were filmed at the Taipei restaurant. This would have been at the height of Huang’s lobbying push, shortly before Trump agreed to let Nvidia sell the H200s.

What could Alice Huang have gleaned – and passed on – during this affair? Plenty. Glimpses into US policy as it was being made, and to Trump’s own chaotic thinking on AI. And perhaps a world of tips beyond the confines of the White House.

Huang was a key figure for government after government as they formulated their AI policy. He met world leaders from South Korea to Saudi Arabia that year; he joined the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, on stage in London.

He would have known the details of the most important tech policy for many governments on Earth – their AI ambitions – because his company was often the only one that could make these ambitions happen. That is certainly true for Britain.

For all the intellectual feats of the systems powered by Nvidia technology, it is Huang’s human intelligence that is most valuable to America’s competitors.

As we’ve been reporting, shares of Nvidia tumbled more than 5% on Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that its CEO, Jensen Huang , was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Further to my last post regarding succession at Nvidia, there’s a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives + Co., told the Associated Press that Huang is “not replaceable”.

“On the heels of last week’s Blue Tidal Wave [in the US midterm elections] this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China,” Ives said.

Still, Ives said there is a risk, as Huang could be removed as CEO depending on the board’s investigation and that it will remain an overhang on shares near term.

Opinion: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish

Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang , the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal . The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.

Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.

There isn’t even a Nvidia board member with the title of chair. Instead, a “lead director” is “designated annually by a majority of the independent directors”, which sounds like a formula for ensuring the attention remains wholly focused on Huang, the sole executive member.

It’s the American way, of course: the cult of the superstar founder or chief executive runs deep and there is a fair argument that such set-ups encourage adventurous risk-taking in pursuit of grand corporate visions. But such governance arrangements look unsuited to situations where the behaviour of the boss is under scrutiny and the role of the board itself is being examined .

The investigation will examine whether Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort” but the independent directors stressed there is now “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

But legitimate questions don’t end there. Did Huang break Nvidia’s internal code of conduct ? Did he mislead the board about his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy? Was the board aware of US intelligence reports that Ms Huang had been hired by China’s ministry of state security to spy on the Nvidia boss, as reported by the New York Times? What security precautions were in place? Other boards in other countries might have insisted on suspending the boss until all the facts are in.

In the meantime, the defence of Huang from elsewhere has begun. “An honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” said Donald Trump . “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” opined Shaun Maguire , a partner at Sequoia Capital, the powerful Silicon Valley investor. Yes, there is little doubt the US tech and political establishment would like this saga to end up in a series of bland conclusions about an everyday infidelity.

Nvidia’s board, however, would be wise not to rely on the “irreplaceable” consensus holding, or the political heat going away. This affair will be trawled over by newly empowered Democrats in Congress because it touches on how forcefully – or not – the administration has been enforcing its own national security restrictions on chip sales to China. This process will go on for months. Huang’s personal relationship with Trump will come under the spotlight like never before.

Will the Nvidia boss, even if he is cleared by the board’s investigation, still look so all-conquering by the end? His lobbying clout in Washington will be diminished. And Nvidia’s shareholders, if they’re doing the job properly, will surely insist on far greater visibility on where the company’s chips end up.

There may come a point where it is in Nvidia’s own interests to move on from the Jensen Huang era. The 63-year-old deserves all his accolades for spotting the enormous AI opportunity for the GPU chips that originated in the world of video games. The rise of Nvidia has been extraordinary. But over-reliance on one individual is also a business risk. Time for some overdue succession planning – it may be needed.

Nvidia ’s embattled CEO Jensen Huang has disappeared from the line-up of two tech events he was due to speak at this week, according to Business Insider (paywall) .

Insider reports: “Ahead of its expected IPO next week, Anthropic is hosting a private CEO forum this week in Montecito. Huang was set to be interviewed by an Anthropic executive on Monday evening, a person familiar with the event told Business Insider. He is no longer expected to attend, according to a second person familiar with the matter.”

Who is Alice Huang, the woman linked to Nvidia’s CEO?

There is little public information available about Alice Huang , the woman reportedly at the centre of the Jensen Huang honeypot allegations , a fact that has only added fuel to claims she is a Chinese intelligence asset.

She was the chief executive of a Singapore-based datacentre company reportedly suspected of evading US export controls and routing Nvidia chips to China.

US officials then came to believe she was also a spy for Beijing who was having an affair with Jensen Huang , the chief executive of Nvidia, the chip company critical to US ambitions to stay ahead of China in the AI race.

People briefed on the US intelligence told the New York Times they believed Alice Huang was recruited as part of efforts to learn more about American AI chips, and to try to persuade Nvidia to push for its advanced chips to be made available to China.

China has denied the allegations, calling them “nothing but smears”.

It is unclear exactly when the two Huangs, who are not related, first met.

Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected within the upper echelons of the global AI chip industry, the New York Times wrote, citing people who had met her.

Megaspeed , the datacentre company for which she was previously listed as chief executive, still describes itself as “a premier business partner of Nvidia” on LinkedIn.

It was in this capacity that the businesswoman was pictured in Jensen Huang’s company several times in 2024 and 2025.

One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted by another attending company on LinkedIn, shows the two sitting next to each other on a couch in Taipei.

The year after, they were filmed together again in Taipei at a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang during Computex, the island’s top tech expo.

Press outside livestreamed footage of the two, seemingly comfortable in each other’s company, with Jensen Huang at one point putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kissed him on the cheek.

The two later left the restaurant in the same car, the footage showed.

A New York-based short-selling firm first raised concerns publicly about their “uncomfortably close relationship” six months ago.

Earlier this year, US officials wrote a memo saying the two Huangs had been romantically involved, the Financial Times reported on Saturday, citing sources who had seen it.

On Sunday the Nvidia chief executive sent a company-wide email apologising for an affair.

He did not name Alice Huang but said he would cooperate with an investigation “regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports”.

Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unknown, and she has not given a public statement about the allegations.

It is unclear what her current relationship is with Megaspeed, though Culper Research, the short-selling firm, quoted an employee in May as saying that contrary to public reporting, Alice Huang was “actually still our boss”.

The details of her career before that are difficult to ascertain.

Several media outlets have cited a profile matching her name and picture on a Chinese fund database, which listed previous jobs at banks including HSBC and CITIC, as well as roles at Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV.

However, reporters have been unable to confirm any of the details listed.

Megaspeed is among a number of south-east Asian firms that buy chips to build facilities and then rent their computing power to companies in China.

According to Singapore’s the Straits Times, it was previously known as 7Road International – a Chinese gaming company with ties to state-backed investors.

At the time of the rebrand, it was owned by Huang Le Limited and led by Alice Huang, the newspaper said, before the ownership was transferred to another company in 2023.

Since late 2024, the US government has reportedly been investigating Megaspeed for helping companies in China sidestep American export restrictions.

The New York Times said Singapore questioned Alice Huang during its own investigation into the company, but released her.

Nvidia has previously said it has looked into Megaspeed but found no cause for concern.

The Guardian has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy

Donald Trump , Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

“ I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it ,” Trump later added, saying he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.

Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the United States, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.

As news of the scandal broke over the weekend, Musk and prominent investors shared their support of Huang. Musk posted “ I agree ” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire ’s defense of Huang.

“ Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership ,” Maguire posted. He stated the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.

“ Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op ,” Maguire added in a separate post.

Bill Ackman , the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair.

“ He is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes ,” Ackman posted. “ He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward. ”

stories.title: Scottish Labour leader says the UK should re-join EU
stories.summary: Michael Marra said he wanted "solidarity, not separation" and accepted that "re-joining the EU won't be easy".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Michael Marra said getting back in the EU should be a "long-term objective"

Published 10 November 2026, 14:17 GMT

The Scottish Labour leader has called for the UK to re-join the European Union, insisting it should be a "long-term objective" for the whole country.

During his first major speech since becoming party leader, Michael Marra said he wanted "solidarity, not separation" and accepted that "re-joining the EU won't be easy".

Marra acknowledged there would be "serious questions" over issues such as currency and borders before the UK could return to the EU.

Last month, the UK government ruled out re-joining the EU within this parliament but Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer ties with Europe.

The UK Labour leader suggested another referendum on the issue could feature in a future Labour manifesto.

Speaking at the University of Edinburgh, Marra said: "The UK should re-join the European Union and Scottish Labour will work to make that happen.

"I don't pretend it will happen quickly. But I believe we should set it as a long-term objective for the UK and that Scotland should lead the change in making that happen."

Andy Burnham will be travelling to Brussels next week where he is expected to sign a series of deals with the EU

Marra accepted his call goes further than Prime Minister Andy Burnham's position.

He added: "Re-joining the EU is not the current policy of the UK Labour Party and not the current policy of the UK government.

"The UK Labour Party isn't there yet. This is a distinct Scottish Labour position."

Marra's predecessor, Anas Sarwar, had pushed for closer ties with the EU after Brexit but did not go as far as to call for the UK to re-join the bloc.

"It is in Scotland's interests, and in the interests of the whole United Kingdom, for the UK to re-join the European Union," added Marra.

Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn't expect a smooth ride Published 3 days ago

UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC Published 3 days ago

Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again Published 13 October

Addressing party supporters, Marra set out how going back into Europe would boost the economy.

The North East MSP said that "breaking down barriers" with European nations would "help Scottish businesses grow, attract investment and create better-paid jobs".

It could also "help bring down prices and generate more money for our public services", he added.

Marra accepted that re-joining the EU "won't solve every problem we have", but added: "If we're serious about growth, we cannot keep ignoring the opportunity on our doorstep."

His speech came ahead of the prime minister travelling to Brussels next week where he is expected to sign a series of deals with the EU.

These will be focused on bringing down post-Brexit trade barriers on food and farming, as well as working more closely on emissions trading and making it easier for young people from the UK to work, live and study in Europe, and vice versa.

A 'roadmap back to Europe'

Responding to Marra's speech, SNP deputy leader Keith Brown said: "Having accepted that people are able to revisit the EU referendum decision taken 10 years ago, how can any Labour Party politician now seriously claim Scotland can't revisit the independence referendum decision taken 12 years ago?"

Marra told BBC Scotland News that he did not support a second referendum, and said he believed the people of Scotland did not either.

Scottish Liberal Democrats leader Alex Cole-Hamilton said he was pleased to see Scottish Labour following his party's lead.

He added: "It's important to offer the people of Britain a realistic roadmap back to Europe. That starts with re-joining the single market and establishing a customs union as a key first step."

The Scottish Greens' co-leader Gillian Mackay said she agrees with Marra that Scotland's "place is in the EU" - but added it was hypocritical to support this while ignoring "growing demand" for an Independence referendum.

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said people in Scotland were "sick of constant constitutional uncertainty" and want "politicians to focus on the cost-of-living, cutting taxes and fixing public service".

Reform UK Scotland's Max Bannerman said the country does not need to re-join the EU to see growth.

Analysis: Marra makes his move - but why now?

Michael Marra has set a very clear policy direction for his party. So why now?

Andy Burnham took the first step by taking his tin opener to this can of political worms at the Labour Party conference as he seeks closer ties with the EU.

There's a crunch summit in Brussels a week on Friday.

But Marra is going further than the prime minister.

He points out rejoining the EU is not the current policy of the UK government and that this is a distinct, Scottish Labour position.

Marra is a new leader and he needs to make the news with a stand-out position, so that also helps to answer the "why now" question.

Scottish Labour believe their leader has two clear roles; challenge the Scottish government and influence the UK government.

Marra thinks he can be influential and it's a change even from the position he held when he took over as leader.

There may be a fair amount of Scottish public support for this and brings Labour alongside the SNP as they both burnish their pro-EU credentials.

Labour and the SNP will continue their traditional battle and now Marra has a new fight on his hands to fully convince his party of his stance as he demands "rejoin" be included in their next general election manifesto.
