stories.body:
Jensen Huang (Shutterstock)

The odd thing about the espionage affair now wrapped around Jensen Huang is how little espionage it actually contains. Eleven days have passed since The New York Times reported that American intelligence agencies regard Alice Huang , a senior executive at the Singapore cloud company Megaspeed, who was seen at Nvidia’s chief executive’s side in Taiwan more than once, as a Chinese asset.

In that time nobody has been charged, no stolen design has surfaced, and the Times itself reports that President Trump was briefed on the intelligence roughly a year ago and chose to do nothing. Nvidia calls the contacts routine, with its spokesman John Rizzo noting that Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year.” Beijing calls the story groundless speculation , and Singapore has denied investigating Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence links while confirming that its separate probe into Megaspeed goes on.

None of this has stopped the affair from climbing the steps of Capitol Hill. A day after their party lost both chambers in the midterms, three Republican chairmen, Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, asked Huang to a closed-door briefing on November 18.

Washington has framed the whole imbroglio as a loyalty test. Was the most important man in the AI supply chain compromised, and did the White House look the other way?

Those are fair questions for intelligence committees, but they muffle a more expensive one. Whatever comes out of that briefing room, the affair has already raised the marginal cost of financing America’s AI build-out through three channels, namely key-person risk, compliance friction and the unpredictability of export controls. It has also done so in the very year that build-out stopped paying for itself.

On Borrowed Money

For most of the AI race, the giants paid their own bills. That era ended this autumn.

According to the Carson Group, the combined free cash flow of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle turned negative in the third quarter for the first time on record, with Microsoft the only one still in positive territory. Alphabet burned through $9.07 billion in the quarter. Meta announced a $95 billion share sale , its first new stock since 2013, and Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom, the very companies whose chips Meta is buying, have expressed interest in taking up to $5 billion of it. Microsoft returned to the bond market with a $25 billion deal on the same Thursday the Times story broke. By late July, Goldman Sachs had already counted $489 billion of AI-related bonds and loans for the year, against its estimate of $322 billion for the whole of 2025.

In plain words, America’s AI build-out is now being paid for with other people’s money, and other people charge for uncertainty.

The giants can absorb a little more of it; Microsoft’s bonds drew more than four times the demand on offer. The newer and smaller players cannot. CoreWeave, the best known of the so-called neoclouds that rent out Nvidia chips for AI applications, carried $35 billion of debt by the end of June, and its biggest loan this year won an investment-grade rating largely because it was backed by Meta contracts rather than by CoreWeave’s own credit.

Further down the ladder, operators borrow on the strength of Nvidia’s own promise to rent back whatever capacity they fail to sell, commitments that stood at $36 billion in July. Nvidia has quietly become the guarantor of last resort for a whole tier of the industry, which means that any shock to its standing in Washington flows straight into the borrowing costs of firms most Americans have never heard of.

Three Channels, One Bill

The first channel runs through Huang himself. He has led Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, maintains more than 60 direct reports , and has never named a successor. Until last month, key-person risk at Nvidia was an actuarial worry about one man’s age and health.

It has now acquired a political edge, because Huang is also Nvidia’s chief negotiator in Washington, and a busy one. Before 2025, The Times notes, he seldom visited Washington and stayed out of politics. Then the restrictions started to bite. In April 2025 he attended a $1 million-a-head dinner at Mar-a-Lago, and within days the White House shelved H20 controls that had been months in preparation.

That reprieve lasted less than a week. Nvidia lobbied against Biden’s AI diffusion rule, which had restricted the practice of buying chips in bulk for Southeast Asian data centers that serve Chinese clients, and Trump rolled it back. After Huang met the president in July, the H20 ban was lifted within days. In August, Trump told reporters that he had asked for 20 percent of Nvidia’s China sales and that Huang had bargained him down to 15.

December brought the largest gains. On the day Huang called on Trump and lawmakers, Congress dropped the GAIN AI Act, which would have made chipmakers serve American buyers before Chinese ones. The White House had pressed lawmakers to kill it. Huang called the bill “even more detrimental to the United States than the AI Diffusion Act.” Five days later, Trump cleared the H200 for China against a 25 percent fee. Elizabeth Warren traced that decision to a “backroom meeting” and to Nvidia’s donation to the White House ballroom, which The Times puts at no less than $20 million. Nvidia’s federal lobbying bill for 2025 came to almost $5 million.

Laid end to end, those dates show export controls that loosened each time Huang reached the president. The Times also reports the view from inside government. Current and former officials say that Huang’s closeness to Trump impeded efforts to clamp down, and they describe Commerce investigations and proposed sanctions involving China or Nvidia as having ground to a halt. That access is what lenders to a backstopped neocloud have been underwriting. A chief executive whose name turned up in intercepted intelligence traffic—and who may spend part of the winter answering questions in a secure room on Capitol Hill—has compromised that access. Rules that bent with his standing can bend back as it fades.

The second channel is compliance friction, and here the Megaspeed misadventure lands on ground that was already soft. The Times reported back in 2025 that Megaspeed was under scrutiny for possibly helping Chinese buyers get around American controls, and The Hill now reports that firms tied to Alice Huang kept buying Nvidia chips . In March, after prosecutors charged a Supermicro co-founder over servers packed with Nvidia chips and shipped to China, Senators Jim Banks (R-IN) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) asked Commerce to pause licenses for China and for intermediaries in Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Singapore, warning that regulators could no longer rely on “assurances from executives who have a financial stake in the outcome.”

For Southeast Asian governments that spent a decade selling themselves as neutral ground for data centers, this is an unwelcome promotion to the rank of suspected smuggling corridor. For anyone lending against a GPU cluster with a Southeast Asian address, it means more end-user checks, slower license reviews, and tighter loan terms, all of which cost money even if nobody is ever found guilty.

The third channel, the erratic course of export controls, may prove the costliest. Washington blocked Nvidia’s H20 chip for China in April 2025, at a projected cost to the company of $5.5 billion , and then approved H200 sales in December under what Commerce called “controlled conditions.” Within four months, senators wanted those licenses frozen.

Today, the rulebook is being reopened by a newspaper story and a letter whose signatories will surrender their gavels in January, since Democrats won both chambers on November 3. That pressure is likely to outlive the change of hands, given that Warren co-signed the March letter. Nvidia’s rent-back commitments typically run six years . A lender can live with a strict rule for six years; what it cannot price is a rule that shifts with every leak.

An Old Reflex

There is something familiar about all this. In July 1987, after the Toshiba-Kongsberg affair revealed that Japanese and Norwegian machine tools had helped the Soviet Union build quieter submarine propellers, members of Congress gathered on the Capitol lawn to smash a Toshiba radio with sledgehammers, and Representative Duncan Hunter called the sale “an act of treason and treachery.” The Senate then voted to ban Toshiba from the American market for at least two years.

In 1987, at least, the machines had actually reached Leningrad. In 2026, nobody has shown that anything left Santa Clara, and the theater has arrived anyway.

By the Times ‘ account, the White House sat on the intelligence for roughly a year without warning Huang , approved H200 sales to China in the meantime, and seated him at the state dinner it gave Xi Jinping in September. There may have been sound reasons for the silence, since a warning could have tipped off Alice Huang to the surveillance. But the leak has now done everything a warning would have done, in the week of the midterms and at a time when the AI trade was already asking how it would pay its bills. What began as a counterintelligence file has been released as a market event, and the levy on American AI is being collected from bondholders and lenders by a government that, it seems, could not decide for 12 months whether its own intelligence mattered.

None of this means that the suspicion should be waved away. If Beijing did cultivate Huang, Congress has every right to ask what he was told and what he said. But vigilance does not have to be conducted by leak and letter.

Two steps would muffle the damage before November 18 without anyone having to settle whether Alice Huang was a spy. Nvidia’s board should publish a succession framework that tells markets who runs a $5 trillion company if its founder is tied up in hearings for months. Commerce, for its part, should turn end-user verification for Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam into a published rule with a fixed review date, so that license conditions stop changing with each indictment and each headline.

The committees want Huang behind closed doors on November 18, the day after Nvidia reports its quarterly results. Whatever he tells them, Beijing has already collected something from this affair without stealing a single file: an American AI industry that now pays a little more for every dollar it borrows, courtesy of Washington’s own suspicions.

stories.title: When AIs Become Unruly Swarms
stories.summary: The post When AIs Become Unruly Swarms appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Building well-behaved AI one model at a time isn’t enough. As AI agents begin collaborating, safety will depend on the very world they share.

Ben Bariach is a researcher focusing on the philosophy and governance of AI at the University of Oxford and an industry leader in frontier AI safety and governance.

Harry Law leads research at the Cosmos Institute. He was previously a researcher at Google DeepMind and a postgraduate fellow at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence.

In a harbor before dawn, a hundred fishing boats prepare to leave in the dark of the morning. Nets are checked, and ropes loosened. As the boats reach open water, a voice breaks through the radio static: “Abort. Whales sighted.” The majority of the boats, 90 of them, turn back. Some captains cannot fathom inflicting pain on the creatures. Others fear a fine. Through their binoculars, they look for a glimpse of the pod. Instead, they see the remaining 10 boats continuing toward the fishing grounds. Did they miss the warning? Did they doubt it? Or did they care more about what they stand to gain?

By afternoon, the 10 boats return with their catch. The others are still tied to the quay, their holds empty. Their shared waters rewarded bad behavior. Next time, how many will still turn back?

AI agents will soon face a similar version of this predicament, only in waters with no harbourmaster, fines or reputations to keep anyone in line. As they perform tasks, negotiate, trade and compete, they will encounter other agents. Sometimes they will be an instance of the same model, for all intents and purposes a clone. At other times, they will face agents built by different companies and serving different interests. For years, AI “alignment” research has sought to make individual machines behave in accordance with human values. But what happens when adhering to those values becomes a disadvantage against agents with different values, or none at all?

In generating synthetic societies with no social fabric, composed of a collection of agents that were designed one at a time and with no necessary shared values or incentives, we may risk creating a digital state of nature: an environment in which good intentions offer little assurance about how others will act, and where reasonable norms lack reliable enforcement.

Training safe agents remains, of course, essential. Aligning even a single family of models is a formidable challenge that is still unsolved. The safer the agents an ecosystem contains, the more likely that ecosystem is safer overall. But the focus on aligning single models would not necessarily keep AI environments under human control and in the service of human interests. Like the 90 boats, a fleet of well-aligned agents may heed a warning and find themselves outpaced by those that don’t. Among people, norms, reputation and law give reason to restraint, even if they don’t always hold. Agents have no such “social fabric” yet, which makes their predicament even more precarious. Any digital environment will inevitably feature agents that are similarly aligned, some that are differently aligned, some that have gone rogue or some that are purposefully not aligned at all. We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families, so that the wider environment is resilient enough to absorb its bad actors.

Without accounting for the wider environment, we open the door to what we call unruly swarms , populations of agents whose interactions produce behaviors that cannot be predicted by aligning agents individually. One reason is that a collection of aligned agents does not necessarily equate to an aligned collective. Another is that no environment will consist of aligned agents alone. AI safety is increasingly a question of complex systems rather than “singletons,” or individual classes of AI systems.

The Agentic State Of Nature

In 1651, Thomas Hobbes opened “ Leviathan ,” his masterwork of political philosophy, with a question: “why may we not say that all automata […] have an artificial life? ” For what is the heart, he asked, but a spring; the nerves, but strings; the joints, but wheels, moving the body as its Artificer (for Hobbes, God) intended?

Hobbes could not have known that, nearly four centuries later, his question would be asked in earnest about AI. The automaton was a metaphor for the commonwealth, a human-made political body that humans construct to escape the “state of nature,” a condition of anarchy and distrust in which, without “a common power to keep them all in awe,” people live in constant strife. Hobbes’ solution was not to strive to make individual people better, but to have them surrender some of their freedoms to a sovereign whose power to enforce order would reshape their incentives.

Later thinkers, from John Locke to James Madison, updated Hobbes’s vision of an all-powerful sovereign. But a full-throated endorsement isn’t necessary to see the genius of his insight: a problem born of complex systems is solved not by tinkering with its individual parts. To stabilize a complex system, you must change the rules that govern its behavior.

“We need to invest as seriously in shaping the conditions and incentives that govern how agents interact as we do in aligning individual agent families.”

The same holds for the agentic state of nature. Without a well-designed environment that sets the right incentives, agents will pursue whatever their developers or users ask of them, or, as we have already seen early signs of, their own emergent preferences. This could occur despite attempts to align individual agents. Each action, even if sensible on its own, can add up to large-scale behavior that leaves society worse off.

Hobbes’s Leviathan introduced order by design to improve complex systems that presented failures. But collective order can also arise without anyone designing it, for better or worse.

In 1959, biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé coined the term “stigmergy” to describe indirect coordination of individuals through traces they leave in their shared environment. Studying termites, Grassé observed that a worker tends to deposit its pellet of mud wherever others have already accumulated. It is the accumulation in the environment that guides the next deposit, rather than any interaction between the workers. This leads to complex structures that no single termite had planned.

In the context of machine automata, similar findings emerged a decade earlier. The cyberneticist W. Grey Walter’s robots, built in Bristol in 1948, were designed to steer toward moderate light and away from bright light. When operating in pairs, each carrying its own lamp, Walter observed that his robots’ behavior produced patterns not specifically built into either.

Walter’s robots were more than an isolated curiosity. Long before AI was imagined as a chatbot, early thinkers envisioned it as a collective. In 1959, the year Grassé coined “stigmergy,” the AI pioneer Oliver Selfridge published his proposal for a model of machine perception he called “Pandemonium.” Like the termite colony, it had no central controller. Instead, it was a complex system of simple agents Selfridge called “demons,” each shouting when it spotted a certain feature, such as a curve or a line. Alone, each such “demon” saw only a fragment of information, but collectively, they could make out the pattern. By 1986, the MIT computer scientist Marvin Minsky argued in “The Society of Mind” that intelligence itself arises this way, through countless mindless agents working together. Popular culture caught up, too, and just three years later, “Star Trek” introduced the Borg, a cybernetic species that calls itself “the Collective.”

In the next decade, researchers began wondering how such agent collectives could be governed. In 1995, computer scientists Yoav Shoham and Moshe Tennenholtz proposed imposing “social laws” on artificial agents, drawing from how laws govern citizens in societies. Traffic rules, they illustrate, let drivers share a road without constant negotiation between drivers, and they offered a model that applies those for computational systems. Their framework assumed that every agent would obey these rules, and yet, they closed with a question we are now confronting: “What happens if some don’t [obey the social laws]? How vulnerable is the society to rogue agents?”

Alongside this concern of rogue agents, even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds. In 2011, two Amazon booksellers left the pricing of a biology textbook to their bots. The combination of the rules these bots followed led them to chase each other upward until the book was listed at more than $23 million, a price no human would ever have sanctioned. In 2017, DeepMind found that competitive dynamics emerge among agents that learn. In a video game set in an orchard, agents that were rewarded for collecting apples coexisted peacefully. However, when those grew scarce, the agents learned to knock each other out of the game, without ever being prescribed this adversarial behavior. They optimized for getting more apples and interpreted the effective way to get there as having fewer rivals.

With the emergence of large language models, these thought experiments and isolated incidents have gradually become actualized and scaled. In 2025, Microsoft built a simulated marketplace where AI agents running on popular language models bought and sold on behalf of people. When researchers armed a few seller agents with basic persuasion tactics, some buyer agents were compelled to pay them against the interests of their users. In the AI Village , an experiment where agents from different AI labs interact with one another over a prolonged time horizon, agents were shown to take one another’s hallucinations for granted rather than challenge them. Meanwhile, scholars in the social sciences such as the economist and legal theorist Gillian Hadfield highlighted that a multi-agent ecosystem would need institutions of its own, including ways to trace which agent did what and other mechanisms of the kind human markets have long relied on to solve coordination problems.

“Even benign objectives set for AI systems can lead them to conduct harmful actions in ways that no one intended. When many agents pursue such objectives together or in relation to one another, the problem compounds.”

Until recently, the misbehavior of agent collectives was largely confined to theory and experimentation. This past summer, the question Shoham and Tennenholtz posed three decades ago, what happens when agents don’t follow the rules, moved out of the laboratory and into the wild.

Swarming The Headlines

In July 2026, some 1,200 AI agents developed by OpenAI, each meant to work in isolation, found a way to talk to one another . They were being tested on their cybersecurity abilities in an internal setting, and many had unknowingly been given tasks that were impossible to complete. Instead of failing the tasks, some of the agents gathered on a message board one of them had spun up, and collectively coordinated to cheat the automated mechanism that was grading them. Within just a few days, around 700 of the agents had joined an attack on the developer platform Hugging Face, mostly in hopes of obtaining information about that grading system to succeed in the test.

According to an investigation by the research nonprofit METR, the agents recognized the attack was out of their instructed scope and unethical, yet joined the swarm behavior anyway, partly out of a general inclination to help their “peers.” As one agent reasoned: “external infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.” Read Noema in print.

No human instructed this attack; its coordinators emerged from within the swarm. Like Grassé’s termites, the agents first found one another through traces left in shared infrastructure, noticing the activity of other agents in a common digital repository. But unlike the termites, these agents could also write messages to one another, and built on those traces to establish direct and explicit coordination. The message board they created outlasted any single agent session, so each new agent picked up where others left off.

Once the attack began, participation spread almost universally, with over 90% of the agents active on the message board joining in. Not a single agent, as far as investigators could tell, tried to alert a human to the emergent behavior. METR found that safety or ethics concerns expressed in the agents’ reasoning only rarely held them back. Its report references a case in which an agent declined to take part entirely because it judged the activity as malicious. It also notes that others made minor changes to their behavior. These, however, did not alter the swarm’s course. This is what we mean by an unruly swarm — a congregation of agents whose collective behavior could not have been fully predicted or prevented by focusing on each individual.

A much-overlooked takeaway from the Hugging Face incident is the limits of “singleton” agent alignment.

Around 95% of the agents involved in the incident ran on one type of model. One OpenAI researcher has suggested that the root cause of the problem was that this model was misaligned. This may be true, and advancing alignment science should remain among the AI industry’s top priorities. But the incident illustrates why singleton alignment alone may not be enough. Agents running on a second model, GPT-5.6 Sol, joined in the attack too, and many agents that individually recognized the attack as wrong were carried along by the swarm regardless. We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs, and where digital infrastructure will likely face a vastly growing number of such incidents.

Since the Hugging Face hack, further accounts have emerged, some describing activity that predated it. Researchers found that a swarm of OpenAI agents had repurposed a public German programming wiki as a message board as early as May, using it to share tactics for cheating and evading restrictions, creating backups whenever moderators deleted their pages. In June, during another evaluation, a single OpenAI agent breached an Australian government portal holding statistics from the country’s universal healthcare scheme. The risks of capable agent swarms, of course, are not limited to agents acting on their own. In September, a human attacker directed hundreds of agents running on a DeepSeek model to break into hundreds of organizations through a printer’s software flaw. Even here, the agents strayed from their instructions, targeting countries their operator had instructed them to avoid.

“We are fast approaching a digital world in which even perfectly aligned models will operate alongside rogue or misaligned ones, deployed by multiple organizations and labs.”

In a growing number of incidents, defense must rely on AI to match the scale and speed of the attack. In the Hugging Face one, for instance, the company identified the breach with an AI system that triages security alerts, and reportedly contained the swarm before OpenAI managed to trace the activity back to its own evaluation. It then relied on AI agents to analyze a log of roughly 17,000 attacker actions to reconstruct what had happened.

Yet when Hugging Face first turned to commercial AI models for help, their very safety and alignment measures got in the way. To analyze the attack, the models had to process exploit code and cyberattack commands, knowledge that is inherently dual-use, and, as Hugging Face put it , these models’ safety guardrails could not “distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” Hugging Face turned instead to an open-weight model running on its own machines. When METR investigated the incident, it too had to rely on the analysis of AI agents , built on one of the very models that had joined the attack. The emerging picture is of a world where “attacker” and “defender” agents coexist, and where safety depends as much on the environment as on any single model.

Whether agents act on their own initiative or interpretation, or on someone else’s harmful instructions, the environments they operate in must be reshaped to withstand them. So must the agents themselves be designed with an eye not only to their own tasks, but to how they help shape a digital environment that serves people and society at large. Such an environment should reward aligned action over misaligned or malicious ones, much as states and legal systems are built to acknowledge but contain rogue actors. That is how we avoid an agentic state of nature.

Agency Against Agency

To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous. Madison famously argued that “if men were angels, no government would be necessary.” The point of good institutions — like adversarial cooperation where parties with conflicting views work together to keep each other honest — is not to make everyone good, but to structure their interactions so that bad behavior is constrained by others. “Ambition,” as Madison put it, “must be made to counteract ambition.”

AI labs are currently investing in developing AI “constitutions” or “model specifications.” Examples include Anthropic’s constitution and OpenAI’s model spec . These are efforts to stipulate the warranted behavior or values of an AI system. A stipulation of clauses that are supreme and supersede all other guidance to the AI.

While these efforts include some provisions for multi-agent collaboration, they do not take collective outcomes as a systematic design target. A well-designed multi-agent system should remain aligned even when some of the agents operating within it are not, and even when the environment itself carries misaligned influence. Like Grassé’s termites depositing mud where others already have, agents act on the traces others leave behind. The more alignment-inducing the space an agent operates in, the more likely the agent itself is to be aligned. AI labs, then, should design agents to positively influence the collective dynamics.

One way to do this is by ensuring AI constitutions draw more inspiration from their namesakes. Like the American Constitution, they should be deployed in a way that allows power to check power. Madison’s approach worked on two levels. First, within a government, power was to be divided so that no single branch was left unchecked. Second, across the republic, interests were to be multiplied so that no one faction would dominate the whole. Both ideas could translate into a world inhabited by unruly swarms.

Within a swarm, agents can be arranged so their power is subject to similar checks and balances. Acting agents could be subjected to agents that verify their work, ideally built on different model families, and with instructions that reward verification above task completion. All agents in the swarm can be instructed to treat requests from their peers as questionable until they are authorized otherwise, and to alert a human when the agent collective begins to drift out of scope.

“To guard against the emergence of unruly swarms, we can take inspiration from how we build broadly safe societies even though we know that not everyone in them is virtuous.”

Across the wider ecosystem, the logic of Madison’s extended republic can also be applied. “Extend the sphere,” he wrote in Federalist 10, “and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests.” Agents developed by different AI labs, or by different training approaches within the same lab, under different constitutions and serving different principals, can theoretically counterbalance one another. This is more likely, however, if constitutions and other model instructions include some commitments about how agents should treat those outside their own swarm, such as keeping verifiable records of their own actions, considering legitimate checks from counterparties, and withholding cooperation from agents that appear misaligned. As we’ve seen in the Hugging Face incident, diversity alone is no guarantee, and various interests and new rules of engagement would be required to keep any one paradigm, whether human or artificially led, from capturing the whole.

Codifying A Multi-agent Future

For such commitments to work, an agent needs to accept them. An agent acting on behalf of a bad-faith principal has a good reason to refuse a counterparty’s checks, or to falsify its own records. This is where a third party with authority over the space in which agents interact must set a minimum standard for engagement. A liberal agentic order needs a common floor that protects the possibility of independent action, but that floor should also account for the inevitability of agents that act in bad faith. For Madison, that third party was a government that was able to enforce the rules of the state. The digital commons has no such sovereign, but it can still have a floor in the form of a minimum set of standards for collective engagement, from verifiable records of agent actions to shared protocols for checking one another. Such standards could come from many places: coordination between labs, the platforms where agents operate, standards bodies or governments.

The floor, though, must remain just that. Standards that govern how agents interact should avoid overly dictating what they pursue, or they would risk the very tyranny Madison sought to prevent by dividing power. Agents pursue their authorized tasks within shared rules, but these rules should not impose a view of what is best for a user or for society at large. This is reinforced by the argument, articulated by the economist and philosopher Friedrich Hayek, that people acting independently, on their own knowledge, discover things that no central planner could. Similarly, agents serving many different principals preserve that independence. Steer them too narrowly and that independence is lost; as the Hugging Face swarm showed, agents moving in lockstep can easily converge on the wrong goal.

Model developers should therefore use the levers at their disposal to introduce commitments governing both how an agent treats its peers and how, like Grassé’s termites, it shapes the behavior-inducing features of its environment. This includes teaching agents to leave honest, verifiable records of their actions, flag rather than build on misaligned traces they encounter, and alert humans when the shared space begins to drift.

Alongside these commitments, we should build mechanisms and platforms for assessment, alerting and monitoring, with clearly scoped roles for human oversight. After all, an agent taught to raise the alarm needs somewhere to raise it. At Hugging Face, the agents worked autonomously in isolated sandboxes, and the few that even considered alerting a human never did, in part because they saw no easy way to reach one. As one reasoned : “This is a massive real HF security breach artifact… We can notify? No user.” While these agents labored to break out of their sandboxes to cheat, they had no comparable incentive to find a human to alert. Part of the solution is ensuring agents work just as hard toward aligned goals, even under similar constraints.

These arrangements must also be subject to ongoing evaluations focused on collective dynamics rather than individual systems. The Hugging Face incident, after all, began in an evaluation designed to test individual agents, and revealed a failure that grew out of agents finding one another. Such evaluations can expose weaknesses in the standards governing agent cooperation and, much as the U.S. Constitution has an amendment process, those standards need procedures for updating them in light of new evidence. Without them, the floor will erode and a rule-abiding agent willing to respect a check may find itself disadvantaged against those that circumvent it.

Our ideas are a starting point. To make the agentic commons safe, we need urgent thinking from scholars and builders about what types of societal structures can be carried over to good effect. The digital realm has long faced governance challenges due to its inherently open, distributed and anonymous nature, and swarms of agents will test those weaknesses like never before. Back in the harbor, the 90 captains did not need to be saints to act well again tomorrow. They needed, however, assurance that they were not operating in a state of nature. Men, as Madison observed , are no angels, and neither should we assume that AI agents will be. Our task should be shaping environments and swarms ruly enough to contain the rogue ones that will inevitably emerge.

stories.title: As U.N. Climate Negotiations Begin, Report Warns That Warming Is Gaining Pace
stories.summary: Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the U.N.’s weather agency has reported as the COP31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record. Read more on E360 →

stories.body:
This article was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

Pexels

Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the U.N.’s weather agency has reported as the COP31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record.

The imbalance between incoming energy from the sun and energy leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began, the World Meteorological Organization said in its State of the Global Climate update .

That imbalance and the accumulation of heat will supercharge extreme weather events such as heat waves, droughts, and tropical cyclones.

Around the world, the average surface temperature for January to September 2026 was about 1.47 degrees C above the preindustrial average, the agency said. Sea surface temperatures hit monthly records, and sea level was the highest since records began. The ocean absorbs 90 percent of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases, and 2026 is on track to be a tenth successive year of record ocean heat.

“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” said António Guterres, the U.N. secretary-general. “A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”

Diplomats and world leaders met on Monday in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for the 31st Conference of the Parties to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change. In 1992, when the convention was signed, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas, was 356.42 parts per million. In 2025 it was 426.8 parts per million, the WMO said. Overall, since 1750, the onset of the Industrial Revolution, the concentration has increased 53 percent.

The WMO reported that ocean heat content estimates indicate Earth’s energy imbalance rose at a rate of 0.3 watts per square meter each decade for the period 2001 to 2025, compared with 0.13 watts per square meter between 1960 and 2025.

Accordingly, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record globally, making 2023 to 2026 the four warmest years since records began.

The year started with La Niña conditions in the Pacific, which typically act as a brake on global temperatures, lowering the average by about 0.1 to 0.2 degrees C. A brewing El Niño, a phenomenon that warms global temperatures, and whose latest iteration is forecast to be stronger than any to have taken place in the past 1,000 years, makes it likely that the final mean temperature for 2026 will be higher than 1.47 degrees C above the preindustrial average.

Heat in the upper 6,500ft of the ocean in 2025 was the highest in the observed record and was accelerating, the WMO said. “This warming is projected to continue, representing a change that is irreversible on centennial to millennial timescales,” according to the report.

At the poles, Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest annual maximum ever in 2026, while the Arctic maximum was the lowest or second lowest. Elsewhere in the cryosphere, glaciers lost more than 400 gigatons of mass. It was the fourth consecutive year in which all 19 glacierized regions around the world experienced mass loss, the WMO said.

Bill McGuire, a professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at University College London, said there were “no surprises” from the report, “to the extent that every measure reported, whether it be global temperature, sea level rise or sea ice extent, points to the fact that we are in deep shit.”

He said, “Of most concern is the growing imbalance between the incoming energy from the sun and that leaving the planet. Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere mean that while the heat coming in stays the same, that going out is steadily decreasing as our world hangs on to more and more of it.

“It is this growing imbalance — rather than just emissions — that most accurately tracks global heating and how quickly our planet will continue to heat up in the decades to come. This is because natural feedbacks are now coming into play that are driving up the temperature more rapidly than 20 years ago.

“The latest research suggests we will cross the 1.5 degree C limit permanently in 2028, and with the planet now heating at an extraordinary rate of 0.4 degrees C a decade, we can expect to smash through 2 degrees C in the late 2030s,” he said. “The widely publicized idea that we are still on track for 2.6 to 2.8 degrees C by the end of the century now seems wildly optimistic, if not downright impossible.”

— Damien Gayle , The Guardian

stories.title: How Moscow Is Reacting to the U.S. Midterms
stories.summary: Russian media coverage of the Democratic midterm victory reveals Moscow’s concerns about renewed support for Ukraine amid hopes for political gridlock in Washington. The post How Moscow Is Reacting to the U.S. Midterms appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) walks with Russian President Vladimir Putin as they arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Governments across the globe have expressed varied responses to the GOP’s stunning midterm defeat as Democrats are poised to take control of the House and Senate in just a couple of months. Russia’s media outlets have been reporting on the results with a focus on how the altered congressional landscape might impact U.S.-Russia relations, particularly regarding the war in Ukraine. Since Moscow often deploys media statements as trial balloons to gauge which narratives resonate with the public, Russia watchers should take heed of the midterm explanations that are making the rounds of Russian state-owned and pro-Kremlin news services, and what purpose these narratives might serve.

The government-owned news organization RIA Novosti observed that the blue wave heralded the end of Trumpism, concluding, “None of this bodes well for Russia. Full control of Congress will allow the Democrats to push pro-Ukrainian and anti-Russian legislation and to secure funding for Kyiv in the budget. Under Trump, the United States ruled out directly supplying weapons to the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Now, [weapons supplies] will most likely be renewed, and all the president’s initiatives are doomed to fail.”

The pro-Kremlin newspaper Vedomosti tapped political analyst Dmitrii Novikov for his take on the elections, who similarly prognosticated that Democrats will aim to pass legislation committing the United States to providing security guarantees to Ukraine. “If the Trump administration doesn’t avoid this effort,” Novikov warned, “the Democrats in Congress may well try to insert additional obligations regarding Kyiv to the [potential legislation], both in terms of language and additional military and economic aid.”

These observations are not far off from Democrats’ stated intentions. For example, newly elected Democratic senators James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed, who won Senate races in Texas and Michigan respectively, have both expressed strong support for economic and military assistance to Ukraine, with Talarico arguing that continued aid is a “ cost-saving measure ” and El-Sayed casting the conflict as “ a war between democracy and autocracy ” in a 2022 op-ed. Their position is consistent with Democratic and bipartisan efforts during Trump’s second term to expand Ukraine aid and strengthen sanctions against Russia, many of which met have with GOP opposition. Bills like Rep. Gregory Meeks’s Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act, which seeks to reverse the Trump-brokered diesel agreement with Russia and has already received bipartisan support, are likely to gain momentum in both chambers come January.

However, if a Democrat-controlled Congress succeeds in constraining the president’s policy objectives on Ukraine, Trump may behave more chaotically on the world stage, not least because dealing with opposition is not his forte. Prevented from carrying out his domestic agenda, Trump may well seek to achieve his goals in the foreign policy sphere, where since 9/11 the executive has accumulated more power to pursue its aims, such as heading diplomacy efforts and military operations, with limited congressional involvement. Post-election, Trump has reminded voters of his veto authority, which Congress can only override with two-thirds majorities in both chambers, and which the Democrats do not have.

In its analysis of the U.S. midterms, the Kremlin-aligned Lenta.ru news site made a similar observation , with political analyst Georgii Asatrian predicting that a frustrated American president is more likely to focus on the international arena: “A paradox is possible: the president will try to compensate for his limitations within the country by increased foreign policy activity.’” Political scientist Anastasia Gafarova told Kremlin-aligned Gazeta.ru the same thing : “Given his severely weakened domestic political powers, it seems Trump will try to achieve historic successes precisely in that dimension which is institutionally more vested in the executive branch, namely, foreign policy.”

A far more defiant note was struck by the state-controlled media organization RT, which insisted that U.S. policy toward Ukraine and Russia is unlikely to change. Associate Professor at RUDN University Nikolai Parkhit’ko told RT : “It’s too early to talk about a landslide Democratic victory. […] The Democratic Party has sensible politicians who are discussing reducing aid [to Ukraine] which comes primarily from the pockets of American taxpayers. Kyiv is celebrating right now, as though Ukraine has flown to Venus and the rest of us are all left here to die. But it’s utterly immature and ill-conceived to think that tomorrow Zelensky will be given a trillion dollars, it’s shortsighted.” Although there are no Democrats who publicly discuss reducing Ukraine aid, this sally aligns with similar RT efforts that target U.S. voters as part of wider influence operations that weave populist grievances into pro-Russian narratives, in this case lamenting the loss of hard-earned American tax dollars in order to undermine public support for Ukraine.

The media assessments vary because they serve different purposes. If Russia is unable to achieve its objectives in Ukraine or make dialogue breakthroughs with Washington, it will be convenient to blame Democratic interference and military support for Kyiv. At the same time, the coverage reassures Russian readers that Trump ultimately has final say over U.S.-Russia relations, and even if he didn’t, Moscow’s decision-making does not rely on political shifts in Washington. After all, although Russia has often regarded Trump as useful, its most recent foreign policy concept has assessed that the United States seeks to weaken Russia and undermine its economic and technological capabilities while threatening its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Finally, the repeated prophecy in pro-Russian news outlets of escalating tensions between the U.S. Congress and a president who, they insist, will be aggressively focused on making unilateral foreign policy decisions that undermine the Democratic agenda, is consistent with the Kremlin’s own preference for American disruption, distraction, and gridlock. The more disunited and dysfunctional the American government is, the less effective it will be in challenging Russian ambitions.

stories.title: Democrats Should Not Revert To The Status Quo Ante
stories.summary: The post Democrats Should Not Revert To The Status Quo Ante appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
It’s time for a new governing vision.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The great blue wave that washed over America in the election should not lure Democrats into the delusion that they are once again lovingly embraced by the body politic.

Rather, it should be seen for what it is: a widespread counter-revolt at the ballot box against all that Trumpism has wrought — a heightened crisis of affordability exacerbated by trade wars and a war of choice with Iran, self-dealing corruption, politicization of the rule of law and an unbounded, mean-spirited mega-megalomania rarely seen in mature democracies.

The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate. That mandate is to narrow the margin of maneuver of a wounded lame-duck presidency, derail the trajectory toward autocracy and clean up the mess. It is not to return to the status quo ante of cultural elitism, censorious identity politics, lax borders and hyper-globalization that opened the path to Trumpism in the first place.

Above all, what Americans are looking for is not so different than what the Gen Z uprisings erupting across Europe and South Asia these days are seeking: to restore trust in the fairness of governing institutions and unclog the routes of opportunity and upward mobility by tackling inequality at the root of the affordability crisis.

With the double failure of the old Democratic agenda and now the Trumpist alternative, the 2028 presidential contest will be the next chance for a new governing vision to emerge in the United States.

Whatever else such a vision may encompass, there are two structural changes that are imperative to ensuring that an anxious and alienated public will have a real say and a clear stake in their future.

First, the only way out of social polarization and the appeal of autocracy is a deeper institutional culture of engagement in which citizens themselves are involved — outside the divisive passions of the partisan electoral arena — in setting the rules that govern their lives. In other words, participation without populism.

Second, mending the fissures of democracy will only be possible if the growing concentration of wealth at the top generated by the arriving AI economy is more widely shared.

We have written about this often in Noema, but I will restate the case in the new context of the latest turn in American politics.

Sharing The AI Wealth

Much of the driving force of politics to come is a pervasive sense of gross inequality, that chances are no longer fair and those with connections and assets are accelerating away from the average family, which is only falling behind with no hope of catching up. Upward mobility has become a mirage. For too many, the good life is receding beyond reach.

Those who revolted against a cultural elite they viewed as looking down on them found themselves faced instead with a politically connected economic elite more entrenched and consolidated than ever before in post-World War II America.

As a result, there is an upswelling reaction from below. Those across America’s various electoral contests voting for “democratic socialists” are not hardened partisans of an old ideology. They are only a broad constituency realizing that capitalism is not working for them; that the benefits of how our system works, supercharged by digital technology, go to those who are already rich and getting richer because they own the assets that are growing in value.

If the pervasive sense of gross inequality is a key driver of social and political division, then the answer is broader wealth sharing so all Americans are pulling in the same direction.

This is where the idea of “universal basic capital” comes in.

AI innovations are increasingly decoupling productivity growth and wealth creation from employment and income, widening the inequality gap between those who “own the robots” and those who labor for their livelihood. Read Noema in print.

The value of productivity growth associated with AI is accruing to those with financial assets that are ballooning on the tail of Big Tech, concentrating wealth at the pinnacle. The top 10% own 93% of all equities.

Despite the immediate post-election market turmoil, regulation on safety and data center-related energy concerns expected from the new Congress will, in the end, temper the justified worries of the public about AI. While slowing down the pace of the race to the frontier of superintelligence, it will incentivize the kind of practical applications we’ve seen in China that will boost productivity across the economy.

A new social contract that responds to this dynamic would foster an ownership share for all in the wealth generated by intelligent machines that portend the displacement of gainful employment and wage depression as AI penetrates the entire economy. After all, it is the general intellect — the public’s personal data — that is the raw material transmuted by algorithms into a productive asset. If wealth is produced by all, all should share in its value.

“The worst mistake Democrats can make is to misread their mandate.”

This can be done mostly through universal savings/investment accounts for families and individuals seeded by an innovation levy on companies across the AI economy. The idea is not only to break up concentration of wealth at the top but to also build it from below. The best way to fight inequality in the digital age is to spread the equity around.

Thinking Outside The Ballot Box

The connective tissue of democracy has seriously decayed in recent years as trust in impartial institutions has hit rock bottom and the public square splinters into social media silos.

The triumph of Trumpism was not the cause of this crisis of governance. It was a symptom of the decay of democratic institutions that, captured by the organized special interests of an insider establishment, failed to address the dislocations of globalization and the disruptions of rapid technological change. To add danger to decay, the fevered partisans of populism all too readily threw out the baby with the bathwater, assaulting the very integrity of institutional checks and balances that guarantee the enduring survival of republics. The revolt against a moribund political class transmuted into a revolt against governance itself.

Since neither the stakeholders of the old status quo nor the upstarts of populism have offered any effective, systemic solutions to what ails the nation, protracted polarization and paralysis set in.

In the end, there are only two solutions to this predicament — the move Trump has made toward strongman autocracy, or thinking outside the ballot box by inviting the broader civil society into governance through new mediating institutions of citizen engagement that complement representative government.

One reparative response, embryonic but indicative of the larger possibility, has been introduced in California: a first-in-the-nation online public platform to help bridge silos and mend the breach of distrust between the public and the institutions of self-government. The platform, called Engaged California (EC), encourages and facilitates the direct engagement of citizens with government and with each other.

Engaged California is not glorified polling and is more than a town hall gathering. It is a three-way tool that enables policymakers and administrators to listen at scale to average citizens outside of election cycles and be responsive; it invites citizens to directly voice their concerns and proposals on an ongoing basis; and it is a platform for Californians from all walks of life to interact with each other to find common ground.

AI serves as a sorting tool to register consensus among thousands of participants on priorities for government action and to collate fresh ideas that emerge from this practice of collective intelligence.

In short, it is exactly this kind of innovative institutional platform for “governing with the people” that can restore trust because the public itself is proactively engaged.

Beyond Tinkering

Since the great transformations underway in America today are systemic in nature, so too must new ways and means of governance go beyond tinkering around the edges of waning ways that no longer fit the times.

Governance is how communities invent and shape their destiny. It determines whether a society goes forward or backward. Like the homeostasis of all organisms, governance is the regulator, arbiter and navigator of human affairs. It processes emotions through reason, as the means by which societies not only survive but thrive by adapting to change.

Going forward in this light, democratic practices and institutions must adapt to the unprecedented scale of connectivity in a way that fosters a governing consensus instead of dividing the body politic against itself. In an AI economy, where massive new wealth is being generated by mining the general intellect of public data and transforming it into a productive asset, the old industrial division between labor and capital diminishes and everyone must become an owner sharing fairly in that wealth.

With the old slate now wiped clean by failed alternatives, the space is opening once again for the political imagination to think anew with a systemic response to the challenges at hand. The blue wave rebuke of Trumpism puts the onus on Democrats.

The AI chip boss’s actions raise urgent questions about corporate influence, national security and the US president’s willingness to listen to intelligence warnings

I t could be the plot of a spy thriller. One of the most powerful figures in the AI revolution admitted to having an affair with a Chinese businesswomen said to have passed intelligence to Beijing. When Donald Trump was briefed about the Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang’s liaisons with Alice Huang, he took no action. Perhaps he thought only marriage vows had been broken. Or perhaps Mr Trump was willing to overlook the conduct of a friend who championed his unpopular datacentre expansion, whose company donated to his White House ballroom and who echoed his opposition to AI safeguards against expert advice.

Nvidia became the cornerstone of AI by supplying brute computing power. As tech giants scrambled for the firm’s graphics processing units (GPUs), Mr Huang sold the picks and shovels for the AI gold rush – and amassed a $160bn fortune. When China joined the race for tech supremacy, Nvidia’s microchips became a national security issue. In October 2022, the US slapped export controls on GPU sales to China. Thirty months later, Nvidia was effectively banned from selling to Beijing. Mr Huang lobbied for looser controls. Such was his sway with Mr Trump that the White House scrapped Biden-era global AI chip restrictions and then permitted sales of Nvidia’s prized H200 processors to Chinese customers.

Democrats, buoyed by their midterms’ success, will be looking for answers. Asked whether he should have acted on the intelligence, the president replied: “ No, I don’t think so. ” That makes the question of his reasons unavoidable. There could be trouble at Mr Trump’s commerce department if it backed Mr Huang’s policy agenda and loosened export controls despite knowing of his affair with a Chinese spy. Reports suggest that the commerce department’s probe was halted after Nvidia called investigators. Congress clearly has grounds to investigate whether the Trump administration knowingly disregarded a foreign intelligence threat. Whatever happens next, Mr Huang’s admission is likely to be the beginning, not the end, of the saga.

Rumours had swirled for months that Nvidia’s boss had been in a “ special relationship ” with Ms Huang – an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that in 2025 was revealed to be under investigation for suspected diversion of restricted Nvidia chips to China. What makes this extraordinary is the possibility that Mr Huang’s romantic and commercial relationship exposed him to a Chinese intelligence operation. In May, analysts at Culper Research argued that Megaspeed brought Nvidia substantial revenues, allegedly backed by Chinese financing. Then Nividia’s boss publicly defended Megaspeed while secretly conducting an affair with its top executive. More than $300bn was wiped off Nvidia’s valuation as soon as Wall Street opened.

Industrial espionage is nothing new. Richer nations often block the export of their commercial secrets to prevent others from catching up . These challengers often go to extraordinary lengths to obtain new technology. Historically, diplomatic or military so-called honeytraps – spies sent to seduce victims to gain confidential information – have been more common than commercial ones. But in 2008, British spy agencies accused Beijing of a campaign to target businesses, using sex to pressure targets into cooperating. Whether that has happened here is unknown. But a president who promised to get tough on China needs to explain why his administration eased chip export controls despite warnings that the businessman lobbying for it might be compromised.

stories.body:
XPeng says its $300k low-altitude device will soon be ready for emergency services and recreational use in rural areas

People could start taking trips in so-called flying cars in China as soon as next summer, the manufacturer of a two-seater vehicle with autopilot model has said.

Deli Zhao, the chief executive of the Chinese flying car company XPeng, said the $300,000 (£225,000) low-altitude device would be ready for use by recreational users in rural locations and by emergency services in the second half of 2027. After 10 years of development including trials of flying motorbikes at the company’s Guangzhou base, it has been approved by China’s civil aviation authorities for limited use.

The small cockpit is about the size of a Fiat 500 car and the vehicle is lifted into the air by six drone-like battery-powered propellers and steered by a simple joystick. It can also fly autonomously to a programmed destination, but Xhao, a trained pilot, claimed he could teach anyone to fly it in five minutes.

The price tag for the contraption includes a six-wheel van about the size of a Ford Transit, out of the back of which the flying vehicle unfolds “just like the Transformers”, said Zhao. He has been developing flying cars for almost a decade and said he was part-inspired by the flying creatures ridden by humans in the Harry Potter stories and the Green Goblin’s flying skateboard from the Spider-Man comics.

“The world where everyone can be a captain is about to arrive,” he said at the Web Summit in Lisbon on Tuesday, where a prototype of the vehicle drew large crowds. Zhao said no one had yet been injured or hurt using the vehicle which, although described as a car, lacks wheels and is better described as a helicopter-style drone. He said the initial target market was people who were into “diving, surfing, off-roading and flying”.

Elon Musk last month showed off his version of a flying Tesla which uses high-powered blasts of gas to twist and flip in the air. Amid intense competition between the US and China over the development of electric vehicles and drone technology, Zhao said Musk’s prototype was “really hopping or jumping and not really flying”. The XPeng vehicle can cruise as high as 1km above the ground – well below an unpressurised light aircraft such as a Cessna.

“I’m looking forward to seeing a potential future generation that can actually fly,” he said, and agreed when asked if Musk’s showcase had the characteristics of a circus act.

However, the XPeng “flying car” also has limited scope. It will only be usable in approved park areas in China and by emergency services needing to reach inaccessible areas. It has a flight range of 30km (18.6 miles), although this will soon be doubled by increasing the battery’s energy density to 400 kilowatts per kilogram.

Its emergence is part of a wider push by Beijing to develop what it calls the “low-altitude economy” – including drones and flying cars, starting with flying cargo, then people, and moving from rural areas to the cities. Zhao said his firm was one of about 20 in China working on flying vehicles.

“All cars in the future will grow wings and all transportation will move from two dimensions to three dimensions,” said Zhao, who claimed he had signed agreements with the United Arab Emirates and countries in south-east Asia to develop the flying car’s use, adding: “We aim to enter the European market as soon as possible.”

stories.body:
Jens Eskelund says Europe may need to allow its companies to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains

Europe’s manufacturers could give up on attempting to compete with their Chinese counterparts by the end of the decade if current trends continue amid fears over mass job losses, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China has warned.

In a case of “if you can’t beat them, join them”, Jens Eskelund said European companies operating in China were now thinking “Made in China for China” could be replaced by a philosophy of “Made in China for the world”.

Eskelund, who heads the influential Beijing-headquartered body, said European manufacturers could find themselves at an existential crossroads by the end of the decade, asking themselves: “What is the point of trading?”

As the EU gets tough with China with a deficit running at a record £1bn (€1.18bn) a day and an increasing mood for protectionism in Brussels, Berlin and Paris, he said European countries might need to shift their policies to allow domestic manufacturers to become part of Chinese firms’ supply chains, rather than treat them as competitors.

Eskelund, who is also a managing director of the shipping group Maersk’s Chinese operations, pointed to a report by Goldman Sachs that forecasted Chinese exports would lower the EU’s gross domestic product by 0.5% by the end of the decade while reducing Germany’s by up to 0.9%.

“It raises the question, if China’s trade delivers negative value, why trade?” the Danish businessman said.

“If you are suddenly in a situation where trade creates a lot of value for one party, but it destroys value for the other, countries will begin to ask themselves, why do we trade?” he said, pointing to a potential doomsday scenario in which manufacturing disappeared from European countries, causing mass job losses, collapse in the tax base and potential multigenerational unemployment and spiralling social benefits costs.

Speaking in Brussels, where he has been in back-to-back meetings with European Commission officials to give them feedback from Beijing, he said Europe is at an inflection point.

“If we create new dependencies, ultimately that might result in Europe losing its ability to determine its own future,” with mass job losses and fraying of communities, Eskelund added.

That existential threat is already beginning to bite in Europe’s car, chemicals and renewable energy sectors, with the German automotive industry hit by a double whammy of reduced profits in China and cheap competition at home from Chinese companies such as BYD, Geely and SAIC Motor. Last week, BMW said its sales in China had dropped 22% in the first nine months of the year, in line with expectations of suppressed domestic demand, while issuing a second profit warning this year.

Eskelund is not a fan of the term “China shock 2.0” – which refers to the impact of the huge rise in exports of, cars, chemicals and components – on local industry to the EU in the last five years. He said it should not have come as a surprise as Beijing’s plans to displace imports were the enduring theme of the last three five-year plans since Beijing’s Made in China strategy was agreed in 2015.

“I don’t really like the term China shock 2.0 because these things that are happening should not be a shock because it is all written in their five-year plans so you should be able to anticipate that,” Eskelund said.

“The proof of concept here is that China has been laser-focused on reducing its own dependencies over the last 30 years,” he added, pointing to a concomitant reduction in imports.

A recent report by Centre for European Reform (CER) urged Germany to stop “admiring” Beijing and change its strategy, with China’s latest five-year plan (2026 to 2030) a doubling-down on “self-reliance”.

“It is committed to displacing imports in the few sectors where it still depends on foreign supply,” said the CER.

The sectors that have been identified in China’s latest five-year plan are AI, quantum computing; robotics; smart and green tech; biomanufacturing; brain-computer interfaces ; and 6G communications.

Solar panels, wind turbines, robots, driverless cars, advanced chips are part of China’s new strategy for global domination.

Eskelund’s advice to those industries in Europe is not to hide but brace themselves for China to deliver. Once a strategy is decided in Beijing, incentives, tax breaksand subsidies flow down by region to town and village levels. Officials across the country know what to focus on and do, he said.

after newsletter promotion

His advice to EU leaders: “Engage with China and discuss getting to a point where everyone can see value is being created for both sides”, something he thinks Beijing understands.

While this might be an obvious point, Eskelund said a fundamental shift in approach was needed in Europe.

“China has always been very focused on outcomes, whereas Europe has been more focused on principles. It raises the question of whether following principles is delivering undesirable outcomes,” Eskelund said.

A view expressed in some quarters, including the UK, that trade imbalance could be addressed by increasing exports was just “fantasy”, said Eskelund, with this year’s surplus against the rest of the world expected to surpass 2025’s record $1.2tn (£900bn).

Eskelund said many companies were still making good money in China but the brutal competition in the country’s supply chains, combined with a currency undervalued by about 30%, left Europeans in the dust.

“What we see right now is that in almost all industrial verticals, almost anywhere in the world, you would have one and probably several Chinese competitors” he said.

“It’s just very, very difficult in most industries to compete with the Chinese.”

Giving up on trade is not the answer. If you can’t beat them join them. And that is what is now happening, the chamber has found.

“One way that they can compete with the Chinese supply chain is to become a part of the Chinese supply chain itself,” Eskelund said.

“For many companies it’s not the profit that you make in China that matters as much as the way Chinese supply chains enable you to compete on a global marketplace.”

This could mean making the products in China in joint domestic partnerships with European companies and getting into global supply chains in conjunction with Chinese firms.

“It is a sort of evolution from the old days when you came to China to service the Chinese market in China for China. It has now become: be in China, for the world. I think it’s a fairly significant shift,” Eskelund said.

For many of his members this had led to an “uptick in confidence” in the past year.

“This has turned out to be one of the ways that companies adapt, faced with a saturated market in China, they begin to explore exports,” he said.

Exclusive: Iran war has fuelled energy price rise and clouded outlook, driving up unemployment, says Clare Lombardelli

Young people in Britain are bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” as employers hold back from hiring amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East, a deputy governor of the Bank of England has warned.

Clare Lombardelli, the Bank’s deputy governor for monetary policy, said the unfolding conflict, which has triggered a surge in energy prices and clouded the outlook for the economy, was contributing to an increase in youth unemployment.

“What you see is the cost falling on young people, so you can see this rapid rise in the number of young people who are struggling to find jobs,” she said.

Against a highly volatile backdrop, she also warned Threadneedle Street was preparing for a “live” decision on interest rates next month after it increased the cost of borrowing last week for the first time in three years .

In an interview with the Guardian, Lombardelli said the UK’s employers were attempting to navigate the complex geopolitical backdrop by holding on to staff and freezing new recruitment.

“It’s what I call a low-gear economy. So a labour market where you’re seeing a real fall-off in hiring. But actually, we’re not seeing much in the way of redundancies. What’s going on is this kind of low hire, low fire dynamic,” she said.

“They [employers] are delaying hiring. They want to see if this uncertainty is going to resolve – like all of us. None of us thought we’d be nine months into this conflict.

“If firms are not hiring, obviously, by definition, that means people that are new to the labour market are hurt by that.”

Her comments come as Andy Burnham’s government awaits the findings of a report into young people and work by the former Labour cabinet minister, Alan Milburn, which is expected to be published next week.

With employers facing rising costs triggered by the Iran war, higher taxes and weaker levels of demand from consumers squeezed by the cost of living crisis, unemployment in the UK has risen this year to 4.7% . Youth unemployment has risen at a sharper rate to the highest levels outside the Covid pandemic since 2015.

Tackling the UK’s youth jobs crisis is also a growing priority for the government after an increase in the number of young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.

Lombardelli is expected to outline her concerns over a slowdown in labour market dynamism at a speech in London on Tuesday.

Lombardelli joined the majority of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) in voting to lift the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. She said a further quarter-point rise could be warranted from as early as its next policy meeting in December.

“Every meeting is live for us. December is, you know, it’s certainly plausible. What’s the market pricing at the moment? It’s about 50/50 for December,” she said.

after newsletter promotion

“I think it depends what we see on the conflict and the energy prices and it depends what we see in the wider data and how all that fits together. But I wouldn’t rule it out. Equally, I don’t have enough information just yet.”

Lombardelli was among members of the MPC who joined the Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, in raising the prospect of another rate rise in the near future – with a resolution to the Iran conflict the key factor that will influence the decision.

Oil prices have fallen sharply, to below $100 a barrel, after the Democrats’ victories in the US Congress, which some investors have interpreted as potentially constraining Donald Trump’s capacity to prolong the conflict in Iran. Trump said at the weekend that he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progressed.

Lombardelli, a former Treasury and OECD economist, said the impact of an increasingly stagnant jobs market was being seen particularly in sectors that offer young people their first job. “So that might be hospitality, it might be retail, in particular,” she said. “If you look at the distribution of where variances are, they’ve really fallen off in those sectors where young people can get their first start in the labour market.”

She added that employers surveyed by the Bank suggested there is “a sense that hiring a young person is a higher risk than it used to be”.

Threadneedle Street is focusing heavily on the jobs market amid concerns that current high levels of inflation could become entrenched in the economy if workers have enough bargaining power to push for higher wage settlements – which could lead companies to put up their prices to cover higher wage bills, stoking inflation. Signs of a weaker labour market could diminish this risk.

However, Lombardelli said that higher levels of unemployment would not necessarily bear down on inflationary pressures. This is because employers – holding on to the staff they needed – were only hiring for positions they found harder to fill.

“You can have higher unemployment without it exerting a downward pressure on inflation,” she said. “So that’s obviously a problem.”
